I should like to answer a question put to me on March 13 by the Leader of the Opposition. On February 13 I informed the house that the government had made representations to the United States concerning what appeared to be extraterritorial provisions in the proposed revision of certain United States banking regulations issued by the federal reserve board governing the foreign operations of United States controlled banks. Earlier this week, in response to a question from the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, I informed the house that at that time no reply had been received from the United States with regard to the representations made.
I can now inform the house that the United States authorities have now acted in response to these representations. Yesterday the federal reserve board announced regulations which do not contain the extra-territorial implications which Canada felt had been present in the earlier drafts. This is a satisfactory outcome of our representations.

On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not be too long, although up to now a single member of our group has participated in the discussion on this act respecting banks and banking, so as to give others the opportunity to express their point of view.
So I am pleased to rise at last to speak on Bill No. C-222 dealing specifically with the chartered banks. I note that more speakers from the old parties have spoken on this bill than on Bill No. C-190 respecting the Bank of Canada, where the members of the old parties were noticeable by their absence.
In fact, we, of the Ralliement Creditiste, were the only ones, with the representatives of the Social Credit and a few independent members, to supply the people at large with information. Yet, the population of Canada has delegated every member of the house to suggest ideas likely to improve our monetary system, the key to our economic success.
In the course of this debate, representatives of the two old parties have exchanged all possible amenities, trying to prove that each had accomplished more than the other and was more concerned than the other about understanding more or less the various briefs presented either by banking concerns or by owners of banks or near-banks.

In the long run, who will benefit from all the time spent in such consideration? First of all, high finance, lurking behind the chartered banks and the Bank of Canada itself; secondly, the people or those who will find the patience to read through the brief contained in the report of the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, because they will find therein the proof that we are right.
Nevertheless, we are somewhat gratified in the realization that, in the end, the clash of ideas begets enlightenment. In fact, when we hear speakers, Tories as well as Grits wondering about the definition or the meaning which can be given today to their "banking", I think this makes up for the sarcastic laughter of past years and gives us some hope for the next revisions.
I want to mention here, to be fair, the very timely remarks made by a few independent members inviting the followers of the old-line parties to remove their blinkers sometimes.
Personally, considering that I have been studying for some 30 years a more rational and more humanitarian financial system, like the one proposed under the Social Credit philosophy, I have never stopped trying to understand fully the present system which, up to now, seemed to be only understood by a very small group. Having been chairman of school boards for 15 consecutive years, I have never understood why no government had ever thought about introducing the elements of our monetary system into schoolbooks.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
Even today, when we pride ourselves on evolution in the field of education, we have not yet ventured to make known to our children the well-kept secrets of the principles at the origin of our monetary system.
I thought at the time that science was perhaps too advanced for pupils to whom we were nevertheless teaching the mysteries of our religion. But I was quite astonished when I heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), former Speaker of the house and brilliant lawyer, deplore the fact that we had not yet succeeded in defining the business of banking.
Let me quote the exact words of the hon. member as can be seen on page 14071 of Hansard for March 16:
It has always been my belief that with an appropriate definition of the business of banking we could have a great deal more control.
March 17, 1967

March 17, 1967

standing committee. I will not go over them again but I would like to say a few things to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) and a few others. I acknowledge the minister's real talents but I regret that he cannot put them to work to benefit the whole population. One feels that he is bound, willingly or not, by an occult power which prevents him from doing what he wants to do and even from saying what he really thinks. It might be an impression, but each time I hear him answer controversial questions, I think he is not the sharp debater one has known. Almost every time, he tries to evade the issue by voicing fears that he knows are unwarranted. Or he says that he finds it very difficult to answer.
Here, without malice, I should like to draw the attention of the house to three scarecrows which always come up in the minister's evasive replies: inflation, printing of bank-notes and interest.
You will understand that when watching wrestlers the most attentive spectators are in the best position to note the repetition of the same mistakes by the wrestlers. And precisely these are the minister's three weaknesses.
Indeed, when we ask him why the Bank of Canada does not issue each year's new credits, which amounted to approximately $1,588,000 in 1964-65, and $1,669,000 in 1965-66, for instance, instead of leaving this responsibility to chartered banks, for the benefit of public sectors, the minister's answer is unavoidably the same: threat of inflation; but he knows very well that if the Bank of Canada issued those amounts, under the same conditions and at the same rate as chartered banks now do it, it would not affect inflation any more than the action of the present chartered banks.
It is nothing but a scarecrow, like those our grandfathers used in their gardens to scare the crows away.
Similarly, when you suggest to the minister that the Bank of Canada should create new credits, based on the surpluses already mentioned, and put them at the service of the provinces, the municipalities, the school boards and the federal government itself, without any interest, the minister can only answer that it would be difficult. Yet, when he authorizes the Bank of Canada to purchase federal government bonds, so that the said bank can deposit them into the accounts of chartered banks, without charging them a single cent in interest, we wonder why that operation could not be logically made for the

benefit of a municipal, school or provincial bank, for instance. And the minister himself admitted that chartered banks could multiply by twelve and a half these amounts which cost them nothing. And then, the members of the committee heard bank owners talk about the high cost of money.
The minister is always pestering us with the threat of inflation. But where does inflation really lie, if not within chartered banks, due to the favours which are granted them by this parliament? And the minister dared maintain, in one of his replies, that all this was done to protect the interests of Canadians. There is a limit to window-dressing, after all.
I want to make this point clear, so that the people may know the truth. On March 13 last, the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), put this question to the minister:
Does the minister see any serious objection to the fact that the yearly credit increase would be loaned without interest, to the public, by the Bank of Canada?
This is exactly, Mr. Chairman, the minister's answer, as recorded on page 13946 of Hansard of March 13:
-I consider that such action would be very detrimental to the interest of the people of Canada because it would be very inflationary, and all those arguments being presented by the hon. member for Lapointe are simply a camouflage for one of the oldest practices in the world, which is the practice governments have indulged in in the past and I hope will not indulge in in the future:
Mr. Chairman, after having brought out the scarecrow of inflation, the minister turns to the printing of bank-notes. He goes on to say:
-and that is the printing money for the purposes of meeting government expenditures.
This is the first-rate argument. The minister does not even realize that the oldest tactics to camouflage the truth are his own. Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I should like to preface them by adding to the congratulations and compliments paid to the chairman and the vice chairman of the finance, trade and economic affairs committee for the excellent job they did in the performance of their duties. The hon. member for Essex West showed his masterful control of the French and English languages, a deep knowledge of banking and financial institutions and an infinite patience with witnesses who appeared before the committee and with members of the committee.
I should also like to thank the many witnesses who appeared before the committee, because their contributions were appreciated in the study of the Bank Act and related acts. I think they have added to the improved Bank Act that we have before us today. I think we were greatly helped by the former inspector of banks, Mr. Elderkin and we would like to thank him.
The Bank Act and other related acts are reviewed every ten years, but in this case it has spilled over to 12 or 13 years. One of the things that struck me is that by reason of the changing times and circumstances a decennial review may be too long a period before amendments are brought in to these important acts. The government should have no hesitation in referring special studies to the standing committee on finance and in bringing forth amendments at any time before the ten year period has lapsed.
The main financial institutions of Canada can be divided into four categories: one,
Bank Act
chartered banks; two, trust and loan companies, which are commonly referred to as near banks; three, finance companies; and four, credit unions and caisses populaires.
The main objectives of our monetary policy should be a sustained economic growth, price stability, full employment and a sound external financial position. In order to attain these objectives and at the same time maintain supervisory control over the monetary system it is necessary that we should have a national approach to banking legislation. In the past the different classes of financial institutions operated within specific fields. The chartered banks dealt in short and medium term lending. Now they are dealing in consumer loans, and after the passage of this Bank Act they will be dealing in long term lending by way of mortgages.
The near banks, such as the trust and loan companies, in the past dealt with trust and executors' services, long term lending by way of mortgages, and corporate services. With the present intended amendments to the Bank Act the trust and loan companies will be facing direct competition by the chartered banks in their long term lending, and are asking for the right to participate in consumer loans to balance this benefit given to the banks.
This is why I was impressed with Professor Neufeld's approach of granting special charters to trust and loan companies for a ten year period, and granting to them the right of access to the credit facilities of the central bank and full access to the cheque clearing system. It is obvious that the different financial institutions are becoming multi-functional, and it is therefore necessary that federal legislation enable these institutions to grow and compete on the same footing.
This is the reason so many members of the finance committee requested that the government take the initiative in the definition of banking. We had before us the definition of the Porter commission which states that banking institutions were defined to include all financial institutions which issue transferable demand and short term claims with an original term up to 100 days.
Dr. David W. Slater stated that the test or criteria to be applied is to determine whether some of the debts of the institution are part of the money supply of the country, and whether some of the operations of the institutions result in changes in the money supply of the nation. The governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Rasminsky, stated it was his own

March 17, 1967
Bank Act
view that as a practical matter the distinctive feature of the "business of banking" is primarily borrowing by incurring obligations that are repayable on demand or on short notice.
These three definitions could have provided a basis for a definition of banking, and with the federal powers set forth in the B.N.A. Act the government could have taken the leadership in defining this very important subject. However, the Minister of Finance gave no indication of an attempt to define banking, but rather leaned heavily on a deposit insurance scheme on a federal-provincial basis and gave some assurance of a study in the near future of financial institutions with legislation resulting when clearer lines are drawn.
This is not sufficient. The need today is for assertion and leadership in this field rather than for hesitation and delay. Some of the junior trust companies that appeared before the committee indicated that they were not interested in the banking business, and possibly the same could be related to credit unions and caisses populaires. It therefore may be necessary to have a two tier system in banking consisting of chartered banks possessing full powers and savings banks with limited powers.
Mr. Chairman, the formula for interest rates set forth in section 91 of the act is not acceptable to the members of the New Democratic Party. It is obvious that in all probability at the end of December 1967 or in the early part of 1968 the formula will no longer apply, thereby giving the chartered banks full control in the determination of interest rates. We recommend that a regulatory body be set up by the government to set interest rates and determine the allocation of the different types of loans that are required in the country.
We have experienced a very wide fluctuation in interest rates in the past two years. At the time of the passage of the Bank Act in June of last year there was an upward trend in interest rates. Today we find a downward trend which indicates the instability in the field of interest rates. During this unstable period the least that we can do is apply the formula that was set forth in the first bill that was presented to the house, in which 4.5 per cent was the base for short term loans before the removal of the ceiling. If we keep in mind the right of parliament to make amendments to the Bank Act at any time and not wait for a decennial review, this formula

could prevail for the next two years during which time it could be constantly reviewed and amended if necessary.
Dr. Slater, in his brief to the committee, indicated the desirability of loan classification into two or three broad classes such as business loans, consumer loans and mortgage loans, with different ceilings applicable to each. Our experience with the fixed rate of 6 per cent indicated that it was not adhered to either in business loans or consumer loans, and we are attempting to apply the same formula by pretending to impose a fixed rate to all classes of loans and excusing ourselves by permitting the banks to add on service charges, thereby making up for the difference in the rates. I feel that the classification of loans suggested by Dr. Slater with the ceilings being adjusted by some formula as credit conditions is preferable to our present method.
I was also very impressed by the suggestion of Professor Ziegel that there should be a fixed ceiling of 12 per cent on consumer loans. It is almost obvious what is going to happen when the present formula goes into operation. Consumer loan rates will jump from the present 10 per cent to 11 per cent to 13 per cent or 14 per cent, and the banks will justify this increase by claiming they are now attracting a larger group of loans which formerly went to the finance companies. The best method to control the finance companies is to increase the amount to which the Small Loans Act applies from $1,500 to at least $4,000 or $5,000.

All chartered banks have shown excellent growth and profits in the last few years, and the profit trend has been upward rather than downward. There is no evidence of any meaningful differences in interest rates amongst chartered banks, and they tend to stress competition in terms of attracting deposits and performing services to customers rather than in differences of interest rates. I rather suspect that the rates of interest are on a follow the

Bank Act
leader basis rather than a true competitive basis.
This is why my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has strongly suggested that the government should retain the powers set forth in section 53 of the act, so it may enter the field of banking and provide a more competitive basis. This suggestion has been followed in countries like Australia, New Zealand and France, and is certainly worthy of acceptance in Canada. In the committee we heard representations for permission of foreign agencies to operate in Canada, and Dr. Neufeld suggested that these agencies should be given a licence for a ten year period. This is in contrast to Canadian agencies in other countries where they are only given a one year licence to operate, such as the United States. However, if foreign agencies provide competitive conditions in respect of interest rates and services, and if competition is a good thing, then we should not hesitate to have foreign agencies operating in Canada.
I have already pointed out the difficulties that trust and loan companies are going to experience if the powers of chartered banks are extended to long term lending by way of mortgages, and the necessity of granting these institutions the right to enter the consumer loan field. Their entry into the consumer loan field would add to the competitive basis of the financial economy.
We in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Chairman, were greatly persuaded by the representation of the Canadian Credit Men's Association concerning the statutory prohibition on charges for the negotiation of out of town cheques. Their recommendation is in keeping with the Porter commission report, which makes the same recommendation and goes on to say that the actual handling of out of town cheques does not involve any significant extra cost to the institutions concerned.
In his brief Professor Ziegel indicated that the boards of directors of the chartered banks were made up of representatives of business, and not of other groups within the community such as trade unions, consumer groups and the like. I also remember Mr. Sinclair Stevens indicating to the committee that more than 30 per cent of bank loans are made to companies which have directors on the boards of chartered banks in the country. Professor Ziegel suggested that the Minister of Finance have power to appoint representatives from different groups within the community to the
boards of directors of the chartered banks who would possess supervisory powers. We agree with this suggestion, which would increase public confidence in the operations of banks, which have now reached the stage of being semi-public institutions.
The evidence before the committee, more especially by the junior trust companies, indicated discrimination within the cheque carrying system which is under the control of the Canadian Bankers' Association. We recommend that the Canadian Bankers' Association act of incorporation be amended to permit all financial institutions to participate directly in the system on a fair and equitable basis.
These are the general observations that I would like to make at this time, Mr. Chairman.

That section provides that if loans are made, for example, to a manufacturer the manufacturer transfers his right in the manufactured article
March 17, 1967

to the bank by signing an intention to give such security. Not only is the ownership of the product already manufactured vested in the bank, but the product not yet manufactured and to be manufactured is also so vested.
When Mr. Elderkin testified before the finance, trade and economic affairs committee he said this as found in minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 52 on page 3524:
In most cases-
-and this provision still exists under the act-
-where security is taken under clause 88 on a moving inventory the bank gives consent to the manufacturer for the sale of inventory in the normal course of trade.
To illustrate what is meant let me give a specific example. Supposing a person manufactures television sets. He transfers to the bank the ownership of the television sets he has manufactured as well as the ones he will manufacture. When he sends out his statement of account for the sale of a television set the sales tax chargeable to it is included in the price and is deposited in the bank. Do not forget that once a person comes under section 88 to all intents and purposes he is a captive customer of the bank.
This means that the bank has received the tax owing to the government. In the event of the bankruptcy of the individual, or if it is a limited company this would apply to the directors of the company, he is personally responsible, as are the directors, for the payment of this sales tax. Things such as income tax are deductible at the source. But what happens in the event of bankruptcy is this. Prior to bankruptcy this manufacturer, as has happened in the past, would issue a cheque payable to the Receiver General of Canada for the sales tax involved on the sales which have taken place, in respect of which the banks have already received payment. The manufacturer will send out this cheque, and the bank on occasions has refused to honour it.
If the company or the individual subsequently goes into bankruptcy, under the sales tax legislation that individual-and this includes a director of a company-is personally responsible to the government for the payment of the tax which the bank has received. The regulations under the sales tax legislation are so stringent that an individual who has no money to pay and who has failed to get his bank to pay the sales tax under these circumstances can even go to jail.

I say this is an abuse. The government is being deprived of money to which it is legally entitled. It is an abuse which has been going on ever since section 88 was introduced into our law. I strongly recommend to the minister that he look into this problem, because on occasion it works great hardship on people who do not have the money to pay the sales tax because all that money has gone into the bank account. The effect of this practice is that the bank is using the sales tax receipts, which clearly belong to the government, to reduce the liability of the customer to the bank. In my view, when the banks receive sales tax they should open a new ledger account of some kind in which the amount of the net sale to the credit of the customer and the amount of the sales tax would be separately listed. The same considerations apply to income tax deducted at the source where the deductions are also retained by the bank. Again the directors or owners of the company are responsible for its payment. Mr. Chairman, in effect this bill is necessary because we have to extend the bank charters for an additional ten years, but other than that I firmly believe this country would be better off if this legislation were not passed because it does nothing to meet the problems confronting Canada.
There is an interesting coincidence in our having this debate at this time in view of financial conditions during the past year and a half and the government's estimated spending in the year ahead. Just this week the estimates for the coming year were tabled, showing a 20 per cent increase in government spending and an increase of about 8 per cent in government revenues. Also the governor of the Bank of Canada has just tabled his annual report for 1966 in which he issued grave warnings to the government.
During 1966 inflation increased rapidly, to the detriment of Canada. The consumer price index went up to an extent that alarmed many Canadians. The increase in the index also alarmed the government to the extent that it appointed a consumer prices committee which held meetings across Canada, trying to ascertain the reasons for the increase. Without a doubt one of the reasons was the cost of money. I sat on that committee, which
March 17, 1967

received briefs from contractors, home builders and manufacturers, all saying that the cost of money was one of the factors which helped create inflation.
Faced with all these problems the government now presents this major finance bill. Does it attempt in any way to answer the problems confronting Canada? It should, but the only conclusion I can come to is that it does not, and Canada would be better off without it if it were not for the fact that the bank charters have to be extended for an additional ten years, following the policy which has been in effect since the establishment of the Bank of Canada in 1934.
Last September 6 the Globe and Mail carried an article saying "The next four months' pay goes for taxes." In other words Canadian taxpayers will be working the last four months of this year to pay the taxes necessary to maintain the society in which we live. The only fault I find with that article is that in my business the taxes are paid first, and what comes after is all one has to live on. In maintaining a farm, a house or a business the taxes must be paid first, and I say to Canadian taxpayers that we are working the first four months of every year to pay our taxes in order to be allowed to live in this country for the remaining eight months.
What does this bill do to solve that problem? It does very little if anything. It makes no attempt to analyse the reasons for the continual overloading of demands on the Canadian taxpayer, demands which have been stepped up by the government.
We saw inflation run rampant in Canada last year. Who really benefits from inflation? If anybody benefits it is the Minister of Finance in balancing his books. To be polite, it is a less than honest way to balance the books. When the Conservative party were in office we heard a great deal of discussion about deficit budgeting, but at least deficit budgeting was honest budgeting. The Minister of Finance can disagree with me if he likes. Had we printed money as this government has done and caused inflation, prices would have gone up but the government, under its tax regulations, would have automatically received far more money.
The government has borrowed money, good honest dollars, and is repaying its borrowings with dollars of lower value than when the borrowings were made. The cost of living went up by more than 6 points last year. The government now is receiving $1.06 for every 23033-893
Bank Act
$1 it got last year, but is paying off its borrowings at a lower value dollar.
The only person who got the benefit of inflation was the Minister of Finance. He did not benefit as a consumer, but he benefited in balancing his books. In other words, if a government wanted to it could spend money wholesale, so long as it printed it and balanced its books, to the detriment of the country. That is exactly what happened last year. The government could have taken steps to achieve greater control with respect to this problem, but it has not done so.
Do we adjourn for lunch, Mr. Chairman?

Mr. Chairman, in my remarks before the luncheon hour I said that this bill as presented to parliament really would do nothing to alleviate the conditions which have existed in the Canadian society in the past year. I listed those conditions. The first was the great increase in the cost of consumer goods; in other words, inflation was one of Canada's basic problems in 1966. This inflation was brought about by poor handling on the part of the Minister of Finance and his whole department and by a rapid increase in our money supply through mismanagement on the part of the Minister of Finance. High interest rates prevailed in 1966 and in addition we had inflation and labour unrest. The government has brought in the estimates for the next fiscal year and we see by these estimates that government spending will be up 20 per cent.
We have these huge increases. I wonder how they will help the situation. We have the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada who gives very clear warnings to the government with regard to the grave dangers in which our society finds itself. I intend to quote some of these warnings. In the face of these warnings this legislation should really do something more than renew the bank charters for another ten years. It does not come to grips with the problems facing Canada. As I said before lunch, inflation aids only one person in Canada, and that is the Minister of Finance. It aids him in only a

Under the bill to amend the Bank Act we are doing very little to bring the near-banks under the provisions of the act. We are giving the chartered banks the right eventually to set whatever interest rate is designated by competition. Arguments can be made on both sides of this question, but without doubt this measure will mean that the consumer will pay a higher price for the money he borrows, which will eventually cause an increase in inflation. Whether we like it or not, the cost of money is one of the key, basic factors in the production of goods. An article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of June 21, 1966, dealt quite extensively with the question of giving the chartered banks the right to set their own interest rates on loans. The article said:
The chartered banks claim to be losing business to the near banks-the trust, mortgage loan and finance companies and credit unions-and it's true that their percentage share of total lending has dropped since the war. But in dollar terms, their growth has surpassed that of the other institutions in the past decade. And the net profits of the big five chartered banks rose from $35 million in 1955 to $85.5 million last year.
The article goes on to say:
No hardship case there.
The main argument for a higher interest rate is that it would bring a fresh surge of competition among lending institutions and enable many businesses to borrow at lower rates than they can now. No doubt some businessmen now paying 10 or 11 per cent to finance companies would be able to get bank credit at 7 or 8 per cent.
But a more general effect would probably be higher interest rates in most categories of loans, raising production costs and consumer prices. The other institutions could raise their rates along with the banks and still expect to hold their share of the business.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The words I have read from this newspaper article support my thinking that what will happen is that big borrowing institutions will be able to get money 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent cheaper than they are now paying for high risk venture capital, but the average consumer will be paying more for money if these amendments to the Bank Act go through. The average borrower will therefore have to charge more for the goods he produces, no matter what business he is in. This will cause another increase in inflation and the costs of production.
We in Canada need not be confident in thinking that inflation was running rampant last July and September but is perhaps slowing up a little now. Inflation was running rampant last July and September and perhaps it has slowed down to a certain extent at 23033-8931
Bank Act
the present time, but we need not be confident that this trend has stopped because wage negotiations take place at the expiration of contracts and contracts are expiring every year. The cycle started by the government last year has created inflation and working men have realized that they have to demand higher wages to meet the increased cost of living. As a result there has been an increase in the demands made in labour negotiations, and this situation is still facing us because the cycle of wage negotiations has not ended.
It was quite clearly demonstrated to us last year that once the government had recommended that in the case of three unions the increase in wages should be 34 per cent and maybe as high as 37 per cent, what is now commonly called the Pearson formula in wage negotiations was established. Today a labour leader is not worth his salt unless he argues for a 34 per cent increase. If I were working for a union and my leader did not attempt to obtain a 34 per cent increase I would not vote for him. In fact I would vote against him because everybody else is getting the increase so why shouldn't I? This is what people are saying all across Canada.
If we as legislators could say that inflation is over and if we could revert to what is commonly considered by economists to be a normal amount of inflation, 1.2 per cent or 1.4 per cent, as was the case in the years when the Conservative party was in power-anyone who wishes to check the statistics for those years will find that the average was between 1 and 2 per cent a year from 1958 until 1963-all would be well and good. But what is the situation at present? We cannot say that inflation has stopped and that the upward trend evident last year has been reversed because, according to the statistics, housing costs and interest rates are going up.
A while ago the minister said, in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, that interest rates are coming down. I suppose he was referring to a statement he made in the house that interest rates on treasury bills were down to 4.5 per cent. But who is affected by treasury bills? We as legislators are mainly concerned about the consumer, and a long time will elapse before he is affected by the low interest rates to which the Minister of Finance referred.
If one had a suspicious mind one could say that the interest rate on these treasury bills has been brought down by the manipulations of the government through securities and the buying of government bonds by the Bank of

March 17, 1967
Bank Act
Canada at a time when this legislation is before the house and we are asked to remove the ceiling because interest rates are coming down. But I say that inflation is not over and interest rates are going up. There is labour unrest all across Canada. The real cause of the labour unrest is to be found in the Pearson formula with which we now have to live.
The Calgary Herald of March 13, 1967 quoted Mr. Rasminsky as saying that the central bank and the government should have recognized the dangers sooner and adjusted their credit and tax policies to suit. He said that statistics on past performance and economic forecasting are insufficient. He went on to say:
The average Increase In wage and salary rates last year was "far in excess of any reasonable estimate of the average annual increase of output per worker in the economy, and even farther above the disappointingly small gain that, according to the figures available, we appear to have had in non-farm productivity in 1966."
In other words, non-farm productivity increased far more rapidly than farm productivity. Mr. Rasminsky also said that we must realize that labour unions will continue to seek higher wages in the contracts they will be negotiating this year, and he warns the government to recognize this fact and to act on it so as to stop the inflationary trend. What has happened is that the government first created inflation and then brought about a tight money policy in order to halt it. This has caused the near bankruptcy of many financial institutions. In fact, two of them did go bankrupt and the collapse of many more would have occurred if the government had not lent them money and thus kept them in business.
I think one can safely say that in recent years we have witnessed the worst handling of government finances in Canada's history. I agree with the economists who say that perhaps we should take away from the government the power to make decisions with regard to the increase in money supply and set a fixed amount in accordance with the gross national product and the population, thus removing periods of high inflation and high increase in money supply followed by tight money and fluctuations in the economy. As Mr. Rasminsky said:
Inflation in its early stages is popular, it creates a feeling of ebullience and well-being which does not tempt the community to ask too many questions about the future.

The tight money situation brought about by the government has caused many hardships to financial institutions, as we saw last year, as well as to industry and to individuals operating smaller businesses or working for wages.
The Minister of Finance has shown a complete lack of responsibility. His only concern is to rob the Canadian taxpayer. The Bank Act does nothing to arrest the rampant inflation which has existed in Canada in the last few years. Not only has it not arrested it but it is moving in the wrong direction. I am not saying that we should never remove the interest ceiling on bank loans but now is not the time to do it when we still have inflation. This measure can only worsen the situation.
Let me say first of all that one of the things the bill to amend the Bank Act is attempting to do is to create more competition among banks. I am all in favour of that but I do not think it will succeed in doing it. Until there is more competition, perhaps the interest ceiling on bank loans should not be removed.
Members of the New Democratic Party have made statements with regard to the interest rate. Although I listened to the statement made by the financial expert of that party I still do not know whether he is in favour of this legislation. I thought I was the only one who did not understand him but I have found out since that the hon. member for Medicine Hat also has doubts as to the position which the N.D.P. took.
We in the opposition urge the Minister of Finance to become more aware of his responsibilities and to realize the effect which this legislation will have on every segment of the Canadian economy and on every person in Canada. We consider that he has done a poor job in handling the finances of Canada and he alone must accept the full responsibility for the inflation which exists in our country. It is all well and good for the government to set up a committee which has travelled all across Canada and heard all kinds of evidence. I have been a member of that committee and I heard the governor of the Bank of Canada explain his position with regard to the increase in money supply. He admitted in the committee that too rapid an increase in the money supply could cause inflation and he said, rightly or wrongly, that as a result of the financial collapse of certain institutions people have invested in the banks which has resulted in a greater supply of money. But basically the Minister of Finance should be made aware of his position and his responsibilities. I hope that in the proposed
March 17. 1967

cabinet shuffle he is either shuffled right out of that department or made aware of his responsibilities and told to take them more seriously in the years ahead.

I have a very few observations to make, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this measure and this clause. I do so because I think it should be emphasized over and over again at this time that there are many people in this country and many hon. members in this house who are not satisfied with the failure of the government to throw wide the net which it could cast under this new legislation to include other institutions than the chartered banks. I am tempted to make this comparison because I am sure it would appeal to the hon. member for Acadia. Within the corral now there are seven or eight thoroughbred banks but ranging beyond the corral are a number of mavericks, scrubs and standard breeds. Nevertheless, if all of them are not brought within the scope of some restricting, supervisory legislation the government will not be capable of exercising, at times when it should, supervision of monetary or fiscal policies, which is very important in the kind of society in which we now live.
For that reason I am supporting the very strong argument advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton West when he spoke in the house yesterday. It was a logical argument, an argument based on legal precedents. I have used the same argument myself. I spoke at the resolution stage of this bill and I spoke when the subject was brought up by the minister's predecessor. I find it essential to advance the argument again at this time despite the fact the government does not seem to be moved by it. The argument is supported by the views of the Porter royal commission. There is no doubt at all that the constitutional cases especially have established beyond any shadow of doubt that the word "banking" has that widest and most comprehensive meaning which would be required if the government were to prepare legislation to cover many of the institutions we now know as near banks.
The Quebec case which went to the Privy Council in 1947 and the Alberta cases which were decided in 1938 and 1947 make it quite plain that if the government should see fit to exercise the right, it has every authority to do so. I believe that the very sensible, logical and orderly arguments of the hon. member for Edmonton West have pointed this out. I
Bank Act
have read some of the transcripts of the proceedings of the committee and note that this point was brought up time and time again by the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. The minister, on behalf of the government, has said no. He has advanced various reasons. It has been suggested that it is difficult to obtain a comprehensive and adequate description and definition of a bank which would meet the situation. It has been suggested that other countries have found the same difficulty. These are not acceptable answers having in mind the dangers inherent in a situation which could come about where it would be essential or desirable to deal with monetary policy and, because of the fact all these institutions were not covered by the legislative authority of the federal government, the government would be unable to act.
I should like to deal for a moment with a situation which has been referred to in connection with an announcement by the premier of Quebec that it is the intention of his government to introduce a measure imposing taxation on institutions in that province. I suggest that we should be very cautious in our approach to this issue. It was significant that this subject was raised in the house yesterday by the hon. member for Medicine Hat because it was a government composed of the party of which he is a supporter which in 1938 attempted, by introducing a measure dealing with financial institutions and particularly banks in the province of Alberta, to use the weapon of taxation as a means of compelling the banks to follow the views of the government of the day.
There is no doubt at all that provincial governments have every right to impose taxation for revenue purposes within the scope of section 92 if they so wish. If the proposal set out by Mr. Johnson is limited purely to the raising of taxation for the purposes of the revenue of the province, none of us can or should take any exception to it. This was the basis of the reasoning in the Alberta cases. At that time the Alberta government imposed taxation of such a punitive nature and so confiscatory in its effect that it was held to be taxation not imposed for the purpose of gathering revenue but aimed at compelling the chartered banks of Alberta to conform to Social Credit policy. I suggest to the minister, therefore, that we in this house have a responsibility to watch carefully to see what legislation is introduced. If it should be such that it has the effect of imposing sanctions of a punitive nature upon the type of chartered

March 17, 1967
Bank Act
bank which is dealt with in this legislation, then it will be the duty of the government to intervene actively and immediately. If the legislation is not of such a nature, then there is no necessity for us to do anything at all. I hope the minister will bear this in mind.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I wish to take exception to the failure of the government to deal in this bill with what are known as near banks. I do not accept, nor should any hon. member who has given any close study to the matter, the excuses being found for the minister. There are ways and means by which this could be done if the government and the minister would bend their energies to them. I want to make one suggestion about the way in which it can be done without in any way involving the government, the minister or his department in the supervision of these near banks, which apparently they do not wish to undertake.
The business of banking can be carefully delineated and defined at any particular peri, od of time in our history. This is the effect of the decision of the Privy Council. Banking is not a static term; banking grows and expands with current economic conditions. Banking now includes a number of activities never contemplated by those who framed the British North America Act in 1867, and I have no doubt that 20, 30 or 40 years from now there will be other activities of banks which are not now contemplated but which will be included within the definition of banking. Banking is a term capable of precise and accurate definition.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
It may be that the minister and the government do not wish to include in this legislation a definition of banks. But, sir, there is no reason at all that the government should not introduce into the legislation a section to provide that no person or corporation shall engage in the business of banking without first having secured a certificate from a suitable official of the government to be named. This would not involve a definition of the term "bank". It need not necessarily involve a definition of the term "banking", because the courts have defined banking and we know precisely what is included within that term.
However, Mr. Chairman, I can see some of the practical difficulties involved. It may well be that the government does not wish to prohibit the activities of individuals and corporations now engaged in certain aspects of banking, who may feel they are entitled to do so, in that they have no opportunity to change

and to alter the economic picture of this country. Therefore I suggest that we include within the legislative enactment a section to the effect that no punitive steps should be taken by the government either to prosecute or to enjoin an institution of this kind from carrying on the business of banking without first obtaining a fiat from the government to do so. This is a practice well known in the country and is applied in the case of many other enactments. For example, prosecutions under the Lord's Day Act cannot be launched without first securing a fiat from the attorney general of the province. Therefore, I suggest to the minister that he take a look at the suggestion that there be a blanket prohibition in respect of corporations. It may well be that the minister might feel inclined to qualify the type of corporation in question by appending to the prohibition some description as to the permitted amount of capital of a corporation or business activity in which it can engage. But there should be no difficulty at all about the government enjoining a corporation from carrying on the business of banking without first obtaining a certificate and attaching a supplementary provision that no proceedings be taken at any time, either to prohibit or to punish, without a fiat first being secured from the government to do so.
The difficulty is, that if nothing is done more and more corporations are going to involve themselves in some of the characteristic activities of banks, and they are securing vested rights to do so. It may well be that four years, six years or ten years from now another government may come to the conclusion that it is essential to bring in under the umbrella all institutions engaging in such business in this country. But this will be very difficult to do having in mind the interests that these institutions have acquired and which new institutions will continue to acquire between now and the expiration of ten years when the next decennial revision will take place.
I suggest to the minister that by Em enactment of this kin$ he would be making it quite plain that the government is not abdicating or abandoning its legislative responsibility, a responsibility which is given to it by the British North America Act. The government would in effect be saying that it recognizes this, and by such an enactment it would be providing that we could if we saw fit, step into the picture if we came to the conclusion that any institution, though not a chartered bank but being one of those described in the
March 17. 1967

schedule, was so conducting its activities that in our opinion limitations should be placed upon it.

Government expenditures are enormous for a country like Canada where everything is done in duplicate, where we always pay twice. Let me tell

you that we are the only country in the world that can afford administrative expenses of that kind; the only country in the world where two administrative services are necessary to send family allowance cheques to the young.
Two groups of bureaucrats. Twice as many stamps, stationery and the rest. This costs much more, and we are the only country in the world that allows itself such a system.
Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that it would be much simpler, in that case, to leave all taxation rights to the province of Quebec and to let Quebec deal with such fields as family allowances, old age security, etc.
And that is not all. Even yesterday, when he spoke about the estimates, the Quebec minister of finance declared that he would create a Quebec housing corporation. Inevitably, that new corporation will duplicate Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and we shall, once again, pay for two administrative services, two sets of bureaucrats. Our administration costs us much more than that of any country in the world because we have two levels of government.
Well, Mr. Chairman, because we indulge in the luxury of such an overheated administration, a much larger bureaucracy than that of any other country, for that very reason, we have to increase our taxes. The Quebec government did it only yesterday, by increasing its sales tax from 6 to 8 per cent; last month the federal government raised its own sales tax from 11 to 12 per cent. This means that during the year, or at least since the beginning of the year, the total sales tax increased from 17 per cent to 20 per cent, so that Quebec residents will have to pay an extra 3 per cent from now on.
And where is this going to be reflected? In a higher cost of living. A 3 per cent increase in the cost of living. And yet, some complain because Quebec workers ask for wage increases. They have no other choice, for the cost of living is increasing very fast because of taxes and as a result of taxes-the sales tax being now set at 20 per cent while two months ago the two together amounted to 17 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, in view of the situation I do not hesitate to say that there is one administration too many and that should Quebec have all its taxes, all its sources of income, there would only be one set of bureaucrats in this field.
If the rest of Canada wants a single taxation system set up by Ottawa, it is quite free

to do so, but this shows once again with what is going on in Quebec, that the Canadian political system is far from being adequate and that to save the money being wasted at this time because of duplication and to give the citizens more for their tax money, there is only one solution: Quebec has to get rid of one of the two administrations, that is, unavoidably, the administration of Canada.
The day Quebec is the only one to collect and spend its revenues, the day Quebec is the only government charged with the administration of Quebec, having nothing to do with the government in Ottawa, then we in Quebec will save fantastic amounts of money which at present are spent uselessly for duplication.
A typical example of that is the supplementary family allowances which will be distributed by the province of Quebec and which will involve operation expenses already existing in Ottawa. We have another typical example of that with the Quebec housing corporation that the Quebec government intends to create. Well, since I have noticed that the province of Quebec is undertaking such duplication, I have reflected that there is only one solution left, that is, that the Quebec government get rid of the Ottawa government in order to save very considerable amounts of money.
Mr. Chairman, the system under which we are living requires, if we really want to act as qualified administrators, that we come to the conclusion I have reached and in which my faith has been steadily increasing, and the more so after the speech that was made in Quebec yesterday.

Actually I have some reservations about the pseudo-Canadianizing of banks by imposing restrictions on shareholders based on residence. On previous occasions when the hon. member for Davenport, the Minister without Portfolio, was perpetually putting forward propositions based upon residence and was talking about Canadianizing, I said I thought he should have the courage of his convictions.

It is so easy to defeat any idea of Canadianizing or any idea of being Canadian when the requirement if merely one of residence, because we know there are very many people who establish residence in this country without their citizenship in any way being affected.
The fact that persons merely establish residence in this country means nothing, because they might be officials in charge of branch plants; there may be trust arrangements behind the holdings or any number of things whereby the actual fact that there is Canadian residence is completely meaningless. I would have thought that at this time if it were thought necessary that there be a requirement of Canadianizing-in other words, that they were going to institute this selfsame nationalistic philosophy-the government would have stated that the requirement should be on the basis of citizenship rather than residence.
I do not honestly advocate that. I do not think it is necessary. I do say however that if the government has such convictions, then let them show they have them. I think there would be a tough shakedown in respect of the requirement; but I do not think it would be any more difficult for the banks to ascertain the citizenship of a shareholder than it would be to ascertain his residence. It is a question of providing the passport, if there is to be a requirement that someone be a Canadian. If this is the intention, then I believe the government should go all the way. Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre) moved the second reading of Bill No. C-37, to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code (three weeks annual vacation after three years).

We were prepared to stay with the government item for the remainder of the day, but now that we are in private members hour, I have this privilege of presenting for second reading Bill No. C-37 entitled, an act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code (three weeks annual vacation after three years).
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, bills are presented to this house the titles of which create a certain amount of mystery, but that is not the case with this bill. So far as this bill is concerned, the whole principle is set out in the title itself.
We now have the Canada Labour (Standards) Code in which there is provision for two weeks annual vacation with pay after one year for all workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction. This includes persons who work in banking, transportation, communications and various other kinds of occupations set out in the British North America Act. It took a long while to get the labour code. It took a long while to get the provision for annual vacations with pay; but I suggest that already the length of the vacation in the course of a year that is granted by the
March 17, 1967	COMMONS
Canada Labour (Standards) Code is much shorter than it should be.
This is often referred to as an age of progress, affluence and a few other things. We believe that one of the ways in which this age should express itself is by providing more leisure time for our workers. During the course of this week we have been spending most of our time on the banking legislation. In many of the speeches that have been made during this debate it has been suggested that there are various indirect ways, such as control of the monetary and fiscal policies of this country, in which to bring benefits to our people. This bill seeks to do something directly.
We are glad that at long last we have the principle established that workers are entitled in each year to annual vacations with pay. We think the time has come, in the case at least of employees who have spent three years with the same employer, for this to be not less than three weeks each year. When we get this bill into committee of the whole, as I hope we will do, one slight change will be necessary. The reason the change has to be made is similar to the reason changes have had to be made in a number of bills this session, namely, that it has been on the order paper a long time. maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENT PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to express my humble opinion in this house on this Bill No. C-37
Canada Labour (Standards) Code Amendment calling for three weeks annual vacation after three years with the same employer.
May I congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his initiative. He also shows perseverance, for this is not the first time he brings a bill setting forth a similar principle.
My personal reaction to a three-week leave with pay after three years for employees in industries under federal jurisdiction was to welcome that proposal. It is obvious that, with technological developments and automation affecting us more and more in this twentieth century, it will be necessary to give more thought to organizing the leisure time of all Canadian citizens.
It is obvious that a prolonged vacation is always useful; in fact, it is increasingly useful, considering the rapid changes affecting us. It is useful for the health of our employees, for the preservation of family spirit; it permits our fellow-citizens to have more spare time to look after their training, so as to reach a level of education higher than the ordinary labour skill required in the industrial field, in arts and other similar activities.
However, when I thought of expressing my views on this bill, I believe at first, I had to study a little more thoroughly the question of an annual vacation for our labour force. I also thought that by referring to the principles of the Canada Labour Code, the labour standards, to the principle of determining acceptable standards and minimums for our average industries, throughout Canada, that the time had probably not come yet for the necessary efforts to be made in order to determine through legislation, a minimum period of three weeks vacation with pay.
I can see, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out a while ago, that the principle of this bill is very clear and very easily understandable. Mention is made in the title itself of a three weeks annual vacation with pay after three years in the service of the same employer.
All the same, the Canada Labour Code that has just been enacted by the house represents a great step forward with respect to this bill, as far as holidays are concerned. Before its adoption, holidays lasted a week only. Then, we got two weeks with pay after one year employment with the same employer.
Moreover, I think it is worth noting that in addition to those two weeks, the labour code states that employers must give their employees seven holidays with pay, seven legal holidays a year.

I noted, as I said earlier, that the hon. member introduced a similar bill in 1965; in fact, first reading of it took place in April 1965.
In 1964, the same hon. member moved a bill in which he suggested that three weeks of annual leave be granted after five years of employment with the same employer.
I noticed, on reading the debate of that time, that those who objected to the bill, such as, for instance, the hon. member for Halifax, mentioned that the government was about to introduce its Labour Code which was since passed since 1965. He stressed also the principle which I put forward earlier, that the Labour Code must set minimum standards, and he emphasized the necessity of studying that question in greater detail because it is quite complicated and in view of the effects that such legislation might have on the industry.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) did mention at the time that the consumer would again have to foot the bill, because when businessmen merchants are compelled to raise salaries and provide facilities for their staff, it is a known fact that, in the last instance, it is always the

DEBATES	March 17. 1967
consumer who pays the bill. He also mentioned the financial difficulties that would result from the immediate setting up of such holidays, as well as those this measure would bring to bear on the small industries and businessmen.
Therefore, I think that the standards introduced in Bill C-37 in respect of three-week holidays after three years of employment, is much in advance of the current practice carried out in industries under the jurisdiction of the federal government and in the industry on the whole.
In 1964, a review appearing in a publication of the Labour Department on the labour conditions in Canadian industries under the jurisdiction of the federal government, among office employees, showed that 12 per cent of them only had a vacation of three weeks within ten years of employment, that is, that they worked for concerns who granted a three-week vacation to employees with less than 10 years of service.
And for all the employees, including the office workers as well as the others, a study was conducted on a total of over 2J million employees, with the result that 15 per cent only of these employees were granted a three-week holiday when they had less than 10 years of service.
A three-week vacation after relatively short periods of service is more frequent among office workers. It is quite obvious that most enterprises which grant three weeks or more to senior employees after several years of service, after a long period of service, require that the duration of the service exceeds considerably the period of three years.
I think that these facts should be taken into consideration. Only specific data about the present industrial policy can serve as a sound basis for legislation.
As regards the vacations allowed by the provinces, we can see that in Saskatchewan the policy is to give two weeks after one year of employment, and three weeks after five years.
In three provinces, that is Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, it is two weeks after one year of employment. In four other provinces-Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario and New Brunswick-the minimum is one week. Two provinces, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, have no legislation in this respect.
As I said a moment ago, the Canada Labour Code has improved the situation that existed at the time, when it was a one-week vacation;
March 17, 1967	COMMONS
now it is two weeks, in addition to the legal holidays that must be granted and paid to the employees.
In my opinion, this is a substantial improvement for a great number of workers.
A proposal like the one put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in Bill C-37 and which would bring an important increase in the standards pertaining to annual vacations could hardly be seriously considered at this moment. The Labour Code having been passed by the government just some time ago, so to speak, it does not seem to me that things have changed fast enough in industry as a whole to justify such a proposal at this time.
The survey that the International Labour Organization sponsored in 1964, in industry as a whole shows a trend toward extending the vacation period in quite a number of industries.
In my view, an annual vacation of three weeks is an objective for the future but could not be realized now. Meanwhile, it would be normal to leave to collective bargaining, to private enterprises, the task of extending the annual vacation according to the period of continuous employment, because the philosophy of the legislation, I repeat, is to provide for minimum standards in order to protect the small employees who cannot benefit from the unions or collective bargaining. We must see to it that, in the industries under federal jurisdiction in Canada, no one has less than a two-week vacation each year. As to the other industries, the matter must be decided by way of negotiations between the employees and the employers; in certain cases, consequently, longer holidays-even more than three weeks a year, could be granted.
We ought to ask ourselves to what extent legislators should go when establishing minimum standards concerning working conditions, without interfering with collective bargaining. I also think that it has always been the policy of the government-at least when the Liberal party is in power-to protect and encourage as much as possible private initiative and to respect our standing within private enterprise.
Where the labour market is sufficiently stable to allow an employee to accumulate many years of service with the same employer, it seems that there is nothing to prevent a union organization from being effective and having a strong collective agreement.
Besides, I took the opportunity to get in touch with some of my constituents who look
Canada Labour (Standards) Code Amendment after labour relations within the trade unions, to give them my views on this subject and ask them their own opinions. According to my little inquiry, it is better, after the act has set minimums, to let the unions act as they see fit and to give collective baragining a chance to play its part.
This does not mean that we do not keep an eye on working conditions. On the contrary, I think that if we look at the policies of this government during the last few years or even during the last session, to begin with, the program it outlined in the Speech from the Throne which set forth many plans to improve the working conditions and the status of all Canadian workers, we find that the present government takes an interest in the welfare of the Canadian worker. Moreover, since then, various measures were introduced by the government, several of which were passed, and always in order to improve the standing of our labour force. And I am especially referring here to the different pieces of legislation that were passed concerning the labour force; indirectly or directly, they are all measures intended to help the people constituting the labour market in this country.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
And, if I consider my area, the people I am most acquainted with, I think we should rather try, for the time being, to provide for sound economic health and, in order to do this, provide work for the labour force by developing new industries and reorganizing the structure of our economy.
In closing, I insist on this principle: To legislate in such a way as to set down minimum standards. I feel that if we consider the whole of the methods applied generally in Canadian industry, two weeks is quite an acceptable minimum since hardly two years ago the minimum was one week; so it has doubled.
I believe the government is acting wisely in this legislation for the time being, and when the need is felt and the general attitude of industry indicates that two weeks are, in fact, below a reasonable minimum, we can then set another minimum longer than the two week period.
Respect of private enterprise. The government must preserve the rights of man, of the individual, of the worker, through minimums, at the proper time. On the other hand the initiative of private industry must also be preserved, for when longer holidays are really necessary, private industry, the employers by agreement with the employees through the

March 17. 1967
Canada Labour (Standards) Code Amendment unions and labour agreements, can extend the two-week period according to requirements.
Such are some of the reasons why I felt, while taking into consideration the necessity of watching over the leasure time of our industrial workers that such a measure should be left to private industry, to labour agreements and not become at this point, the subject matter of an act of parliament.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I made myself clear but what I meant to say once again is that the government provides a minimum of two weeks to protect the small employee who cannot join a labour union and is thus unprotected. The government sets up a minimum so as not to unbalance its economy and leaves private enterprise free. When I speak of private enterprise, I mean the employer as well as the employees who can discuss things together. I mean that through collective agreements, they can provide for the vacation periods which they feel can be granted to the employees. The initiative is left to the employers and the employees and I think that that is in the spirit of the labour code. I think it was in that spirit that the labour code was passed by the house not very long ago.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENT PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak with the intention of taking only a minute or two, realizing that other members wish to express themselves on this worth-while legislation before us. I must admit that in the first instance I hoped this legislation would also apply to members of parliament. It would be nice if we could be assured of at least a three-week holiday in which to recuperate from the vicissitudes and involvements in this place and others.
I must say also that I cannot go along with the comments of the hon. member for Rimouski, who suggested that the time is not yet ripe for making an advance with this kind of legislation, and that we ought to ensure that there are minimum standards for vacation time, particularly for those people in the labouring sector who very likely need holidays more than any other people.

All of us, whether we sit in this place or not, are aware that there are increasing pressures today on family life, that society is developing to a state in which it is not possible much of the time for members of families to be together because of vocational commitments and commitments beyond one's vocational life. If is almost true to say that in many instances members of families do not know each other well. They do not enjoy the day to day contact which is needed for a strong family life.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is also true that the pressures of the business world are such that it is often impossible for people to get the kind of recreation which is needed week by week to allow them to restore themselves and carry on their chosen endeavours. I think it is necessary today for people to have much longer than the two weeks normally accepted as the minimum standard. I think it is true to say also that those who belong to the professional classes and who have reached some degree of independence in the business world no longer worry about these things. It is common enough for professional people in many walks of life to take vacations extending as long as two months. They feel they need this and that it is justified. I know of doctors, I know of lawyers, and I even know of some of my colleagues in the ministry who make sure they spend two months each year on vacation.
Here we are talking about people who are not self-employed, people who are often not members of a professional group, and who are allowed, in most cases, two weeks as a minimum. I think it is important that amendments be made to the labour code setting the minimum standard so as to provide for at least three weeks. While it may not be possible to take action this afternoon in this regard, I do hope this question will be given serious consideration by the government.
In confirming my support for this bill I wish, however, to put forward a word of caution. I believe that increasingly we shall be facing a problem of which this bill gives only an inkling

the redefinition of the meaning of work and of leisure. I have heard social scientists make confident predictions that by the end of this century the normal vacation period will be eight weeks. Some of us will relish the thought of reaching that date, if indeed we do. As the affluent society becomes more and more productive it will no longer be necessary for people to continue to work as hard as they have done in previous years.
March 17. 1967

Indeed it might be harmful to the economy were they to do so. This means longer periods of leisure for all of us, and greater opportunities for vacations.
One might think that everyone would be pleased with such a prospect, but in a number of instances such is not the case. Indeed many people today who have found themselves with increasing leisure have reacted by seeking other employment. The word moonlighting has come into our vocabulary to describe this activity. It seems to me we have schooled ourselves so well to work that we have not yet learned how to use leisure creatively. We have developed people with neuroses about the fact that they are not allowed to work as hard or as long as they once were.
I hope that in the next generation or so serious thought will be given by social scientists, people concerned with labour codes and so on, to the effects on man of having his work load diminished and replaced by longer periods of leisure. Surely our leisure time must not be spent huddled in front of a television set with a can of beer. Yet this is the picture which will increasingly be true of many Canadians if we cannot adduce other possibilities which are more interesting in terms of human development and interaction.
In asking for a minimum standard of three weeks we are asking for opportunity; but we are also endangering the sanity of many who have not yet learned how to handle leisure creatively. Our problem stems from the fact that the notion of work, according to our concepts, is primarily tied to the making of money and not to participating in some creative act. If we can make the transition in our generation from work being related to money to work being related to creative output, something exciting will happen in our society. If not, I am afraid we shall become a very depressing, work-orientated, unhappy society which has little hope before it, even if this period is extended to three weeks.

speechtext:
I was not referring to any other speech maker. The hon. member always does an excellent job tearing mine apart. If we are to assess legislation of this nature we should review what has been done in the past by the federal government and the provinces. By law, annual vacations with pay in industries subject to federal jurisdiction have been provided since 1958. The first federal statute required employers falling within its scope to grant employees a paid week's vacation after one year of employment, and two weeks after two years of service. Hon. members will recall that act was replaced by Part III of the celebrated Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
The Labour (Standards) Code provides for vacations with pay of at least two weeks after every completed year of employment, and vacation pay is 4 per cent of wages for the year in which an employee establishes his claim to vacation. Under the federal law a year of employment must be continuous with one employer, and may be a 12 month period commencing with the day the employee began to work or any subsequent anniversary of that date. It may be a calendar year or any other year approved by the Minister of Labour.
All the provinces, with the exception of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, have annual vacation laws. We can appreciate why P.E.I. does not have such law because it is predominantly an agricultural province, while in Newfoundland the labour unions have not been as well organized and have not
DEBATES	March 17. 1967
had the time in which to mature that they have had in other provinces. Provisions for annual vacations with pay are contained in the Alberta labour act and in orders under the Ontario hours of work act, and in Quebec under minimum wage orders Nos. 3, 7 and 39. They are also governed by the Quebec collective agreements act.
The Canada Labour (Standards) Code applies to industries within federal jurisdiction, and the only employees excluded are engineers, superintendents and others who exercise management functions, as well as members of the medical, dental, architectural and legal professions. The provincial laws govern employees in employment within the jurisdiction of the provinces, with the exception of certain classes of employees who are otherwise noted.
In all provinces farm workers are excluded. Horticultural workers are excluded in British Columbia, and workers employed in the growing of flowers, fruit and vegetables in Ontario. Market garden workers are excluded in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Employees of municipal and school corporations in Quebec are excluded, and members of family undertakings in Saskatchewan. Salesmen are excluded in Alberta, Ontario and Saskatchewan, but in Quebec their exclusion is limited to those with less than the three months work, and those who work for two or more employers at the same time.
Exemptions are necessary in all provinces, and if this house were to provide blanket legislation it would create a problem for industry, particularly industries operating on a very close margin.
